Tan-Surya Family ancestral_origin Fujian province, China place. Record status: current. This line is the

HOW TO READ THIS CHART
- Dates are Western calendar. Where the Chinese calendar year was the only one
  recorded, it is given in brackets, e.g., (光緒 廿三年) for 1897.
- A dash (—) in a death column means the person was alive as of the last update
  (1 Feb 2024) or that the death date is not yet confirmed. A question mark (?) 
  means the record is missing or illegible.
- Marriage entries are listed under the male partner's row only when the female
  partner's line is kept in her own family's chart. This is an old convention and
  is kept for continuity; do not take it as a judgement about the marriage.
- Handwritten annotations in Chinese are given in the Remarks column in
  parentheses. Those in English are given as-is.
- Branch letters: A = eldest son's line, B = second son's line, C = third son's
  line, D = daughter's line (used only from 1920 onward; earlier daughters are
  listed in the family book, not this chart).

Archive item 3: Tan-Surya Family Bible Records
Source format: Family Bible

1877, January 8. Tan Kim Swee, born half an hour after his brother Kim Chuan. The twins were small but healthy.

1879, October 23. Tan Bee Eng, daughter, born at dusk. (Note in margin, in different ink: "Bee Eng married Goh Cheng Huat of Malacca in 1902, and went to live there.")

1882, May 30. Tan Ah Seng, the second son, died of fever. He was 7 years old.

1885, February 11. Tan Kim Chuan, aged 8, drowned in the river behind the godown. A great sorrow to us. (Margin note: "The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away.")

1889, September 17. Tan Ah Kow married Lim Chwee Neo, daughter of Lim Cheng Tee of Telok Ayer. The marriage was solemnised by the Reverend W. F. Oldham at the Prinsep Street Church. (Margin note, later hand: "Chwee Neo died 1897, childless. Ah Kow married again in 1898, see below.")

1890, June 21. Tan Boon Teck, my grandfather, died aged 72. Buried at the Christian cemetery near Fort Canning.

1891, April 3. Tan Ah Kow and Lim Chwee Neo had a stillborn son. The child was unnamed.

1893, November 12. Tan Siew Lan, daughter of Tan Ah Kow and Lim Chwee Neo, born. She was a delicate girl.

1897, August 8. Lim Chwee Neo, wife of Tan Ah Kow, died of consumption. She was 29 years old. Buried at Bidadari.

1898, June 12. Tan Ah Kow married Surya binte Hassan, daughter of Hassan bin Omar of Geylang. The marriage was at the Registry of Marriages, Fort Canning. (This Bible was given to them on this day.)

1899, February 27. Tan Boon Teck, my father, died in his sleep. He was 81.

1900, January 15. Tan Ah Kow and Surya binte Hassan had a son, named Tan Boon Keng. Born at 6 in the morning.

1902, October 5. Tan Siew Lan, daughter of Tan Ah Kow and first wife Chwee Neo, died of dysentery. She was 9 years old.

1903, April 22. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a daughter, Tan Swee Lian. Born at 2 in the afternoon.

1905, July 30. Tan Boon Keng, son of Ah Kow, aged 5, died of cholera. A terrible year in Singapore.

1907, January 19. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a son, Tan Kim Hock.

1910, September 8. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a daughter, Tan Geok Eng.

1912, November 3. Tan Ah Kow's mother, Surya binte Abdullah, died aged 76. She was the matriarch of our family.

1915, June 20. Tan Kim Hock, son of Ah Kow, aged 8, died of injuries from a cart accident on the road to Geylang.

1918, December 15. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a son, Tan Cheng Huat. (Margin note: "Born during the great influenza, but the Lord spared him.")

Tan Ah Kow birth_date 1871-03-14 date. Record status: current.

1920, February 2. Tan Boon Teck, the eldest son of Ah Kow, married Lee Geok Hwa, daughter of Lee Chin Seng of River Valley.

1921, August 18. Tan Geok Eng, daughter of Ah Kow, married Wee Kim Yam of Serangoon.

1923, January 30. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a daughter, Tan Hai Neo. Their last child.

1924, June 1. Tan Boon Keng, the second son of Ah Kow, died in a motor car accident on the Bukit Timah Road. He was 24 years old.

1926, November 11. Tan Cheng Huat, son of Ah Kow, married Goh Lian Neo, daughter of Goh Cheng Huat and Tan Bee Eng of Malacca. Thus the families were joined again.

1928, March 25. Tan Ah Kow and Surya celebrated their 30th wedding anniversary. A great gathering was held at the house on Kampong Glam. All the children and grandchildren were present, except those who had passed on.

RECORD OF DEATHS

1873, September 30. Tan Ah Lian, daughter of Tan Boon Teck, aged 1 year.

1882, May 30. Tan Ah Seng, second son of Tan Boon Teck, aged 7.

1885, February 11. Tan Kim Chuan, aged 8. Drowned.

1890, June 21. Tan Boon Teck, aged 72.

1897, August 8. Lim Chwee Neo, wife of Tan Ah Kow, aged 29.

1897, December 1. Tan Ah Kow's infant son, stillborn, would have been named Tan Boon Han.

1898, February 14. Tan Kim Swee, the twin, died of fever aged 21. He never married.

1899, February 27. Tan Boon Teck, the elder, aged 81.

1902, October 5. Tan Siew Lan, aged 9.

1905, July 30. Tan Boon Keng, aged 5.

1912, November 3. Surya binte Abdullah, aged 76.

1915, June 20. Tan Kim Hock, aged 8.
RECORD OF MARRIAGES (continued)

1920, February 2. Tan Boon Teck, eldest son of Ah Kow, to Lee Geok Hwa, daughter of Lee Chin Seng of River Valley. The ceremony was held at the bride's family home, with a feast that lasted till midnight. †

1921, August 18. Tan Geok Eng, daughter of Ah Kow, to Wee Kim Yam of Serangoon. The groom's family sent a fine roast pig and two baskets of oranges. †

1926, November 11. Tan Cheng Huat, son of Ah Kow, to Goh Lian Neo, daughter of Goh Cheng Huat and Tan Bee Eng of Malacca. Thus the families were joined again. The bride came with her mother and two aunts, and they stayed a week. †

1929, June 8. Tan Hai Neo, youngest daughter of Ah Kow, to Lim Keng Seng, third son of Lim Boon Tat of Pasir Panjang. The groom is a clerk at the harbour office. The marriage was quiet, as Hai Neo wished it. †

1930, January 1. Tan Ah Kow, widower of the late Lim Chwee Neo, married Tan Siew Lan of Geylang. The ceremony took place at the registry office on Fort Canning, with only the two families present. The marriage certificate names Tan Siew Lan as the spouse of Tan Ah Kow. Record status: current. A small reception was held afterwards at the house on Kampong Glam. The children were not all in favour, but they came. †

1930, March 12. Tan Cheng Huat and Goh Lian Neo had a son, Tan Boon Chye. The first grandchild of the new marriage. (Margin note: "A fine boy, born on a Thursday.")

1930, June 1. Tan Boon Teck and Lee Geok Hwa had a daughter, Tan Swee Lian. She was named after her step-grandmother, which caused some talk.

1930, September 18. Tan Hai Neo and Lim Keng Seng had a daughter, Lim Siew Tin. Born at the Kandang Kerbau Hospital.

FAMILY NOTES

The marriage of Ah Kow and Siew Lan in 1930 was a matter of some debate among the older members of the family. Siew Lan had been a friend of the family for many years, and had helped nurse Ah Kow's mother in her last illness. Some said it was too soon after the death of Lim Chwee Neo, but that was more than thirty years ago. The children were grown and had their own households.

Siew Lan was born in 1898, the daughter of Tan Siew Lan (senior) and Lim Ah Moy of Geylang. She was a dressmaker and kept a small shop on Arab Street before her marriage. She had never been married before.

The registry office ceremony was a departure from the usual family practice. The older weddings were all held at home with the appropriate rites, but Ah Kow said he had had enough of large gatherings after the anniversary celebration. The certificate was signed by the Registrar, a Mr. P. J. O'Sullivan, and witnessed by Tan Boon Teck and Goh Lian Neo.

1930, October 12. Ah Kow and Siew Lan had a son, Tan Boon Hock. Born at home on Kampong Glam, with the midwife Mrs. D'Souza in attendance. A healthy child, weighing eight pounds.

1930, December 25. Christmas dinner at the Kampong Glam house. All the children came, and the new baby was shown to the assembled family. Tan Boon Teck made a speech about the past year and the changes it had brought. The photograph taken that day shows Ah Kow holding the baby, with Siew Lan beside him and the grandchildren seated on the floor. (Margin note: "Keep this picture safe.")

MEMORANDA

1931, February 14. It was discovered that the marriage certificate of Ah Kow and Siew Lan had been mislaid. A search was made of the house, and it was found in a drawer of the writing desk, under some old bills. The certificate is now kept in the tin box with the other important papers.

1931, March 3. Ah Kow made a new will. The house on Kampong Glam is to pass to Siew Lan for her lifetime, and then to the children of his first marriage, in equal shares. The children of the second marriage, namely Tan Boon Hock, shall have a sum of money set aside for his education. The will was witnessed by Lim Keng Seng and Lee Geok Hwa.

1931, June 18. Siew Lan gave birth to a daughter, stillborn. She was named Tan Siew Tin. The child was buried in the family plot at Bidadari.

1931, August 30. Ah Kow's health began to fail. He had a cough that would not go away, and the doctor, a Dr. Chelliah, advised him to rest. He spent most of September at the house, sitting in the verandah and watching the traffic on Kampong Glam.
1932, January 5. Ah Kow was taken to the Singapore General Hospital, where Dr. Chelliah examined him again. The cough had worsened, and there was some blood in the sputum. Dr. Chelliah said it was consumption, and that the climate here was not good for him. He advised a long sea voyage, but Ah Kow refused, saying he was too old to travel.

1932, February 2. Tan Boon Teck came from Penang to see his father. He stayed a week. During this time he and Siew Lan had a disagreement about the will. Boon Teck felt that the house should pass directly to him and his siblings, and that the provision for Boon Hock's education was too generous. Siew Lan said the will was Ah Kow's own wish, and she would not see it changed. The matter was not resolved, and Boon Teck returned to Penang on the 9th.

1932, March 14. Ah Kow seemed a little better. He sat up in his chair and asked for the family Bible to be brought to him. He looked through the pages for a long time, especially at the entries from his youth. He pointed to the entry for his first wife, Lim Neo, and said, "She was a good woman." He then asked Siew Lan to write down the date of his own birth, which she did, though she noted in the margin that he had always said it was a year earlier than the record showed.

1932, April 1. Ah Kow took a turn for the worse. The family was sent for. Tan Boon Teck arrived from Penang on the 3rd, and the daughters, Swee Eng and Swee Lian, came with their husbands. Ah Kow was conscious but weak. He asked to see the baby, Boon Hock, and held him for a few minutes.

1932, April 6. Ah Kow died at half past six in the evening. The cause of death was given as consumption. He was in his seventy-third year, according to the family record, though there was some dispute about the exact year of his birth, as noted above. The funeral was held on the 8th, at Bidadari, where he was buried beside his first wife, Lim Neo. The service was conducted by the Rev. Mr. Goh, of the Methodist Church. A large number of people attended, including many from the old neighbourhood in Kampong Glam.

1932, April 15. The will was read by Mr. Lim Keng Seng, the lawyer who had witnessed it. The terms were as Ah Kow had set them out in March of the previous year. Siew Lan was to have the house for her lifetime, and then it was to go to the children of the first marriage, in equal shares. Boon Hock was to have a sum of two thousand dollars set aside for his education. There was some grumbling from Boon Teck, but he did not contest the will.

1932, May 20. Siew Lan decided to sell the house on Kampong Glam. She said she could not bear to live there alone, and the memories were too many. She moved to a smaller house in Geylang, taking Boon Hock with her. The sale was completed in August, and the proceeds were invested, with the income to be used for Boon Hock's upkeep.

1932, September 1. Siew Lan wrote to her sister in Malacca, describing the move. The letter was kept in the tin box with the other papers. In it she said that the new house was smaller, but that it had a good garden, and that Boon Hock was thriving. She also mentioned that she had not heard from Boon Teck since the sale, and that she hoped he would not hold a grudge.

1933, January 10. Tan Boon Teck wrote to Siew Lan from Penang. The letter was polite but cool. He said that he and his siblings had agreed to allow Siew Lan to live in the Geylang house for the rest of her life, even though the will had only provided for the Kampong Glam house. He said this was in recognition of the care she had given their father. Siew Lan was grateful, and wrote back to thank him.

1933, March 18. A note in the Bible, in Siew Lan's hand: "Today I went to Bidadari and put flowers on the grave. The grass has grown over the mound, and the stone is clean. I also put flowers on the small grave of Siew Tin, who is beside her father. I will go every year on this day."

1934, June 5. Boon Hock started school, at the Anglo-Chinese School. He was a bright boy, and his teacher, a Mr. Tan, said he showed promise in arithmetic. Siew Lan was proud, and wrote the date in the Bible, under the entry for his birth.

documents.title: Visitor Log 1987-1988
documents.content:
**3 January 1987 (Sat)**
09:45 – Mr. Rajendran s/o Muthiah, self-employed. Purpose: general visit, viewed exhibition hall. Signed guest book.
11:20 – Group of 12 students from Raffles Institution, accompanied by Mr. Goh Seng Tat (teacher). Purpose: school project on local heritage. Given brief tour by duty officer. Students asked many questions about the shophouse restoration. Mr. Goh requested a follow-up visit for the History Society in March.

**5 January 1987 (Mon)**
15:05 – Dr. Patricia Lim, University of Malaya, Department of History. Purpose: research on early Chinese clan associations in Singapore. Requested access to the Tan family papers (restricted collection). Application form given; advised of 2-week processing time.

**6 January 1987 (Tue)**
No visitors. Staff training on new catalogue system (part 1 of 3).

**7 January 1987 (Wed)**
10:30 – Mr. & Mrs. Koh Choon Seng, members of the public. Purpose: tracing family connection to the Surya family through marriage records. Assisted by M. Surya (volunteer). No records found in current index; suggested they return after the microfilm reader is installed (expected March).

**8 January 1987 (Thu)**
14:00 – Mr. William Ng, freelance journalist, *The Straits Times*. Purpose: background interview for an article on the new Centre. Spoke with Director (Mr. Tan) for 45 minutes. Requested photographs of the reading room; permission granted for non-flash photography.

**9 January 1987 (Fri)**
09:20 – Madam Lim Siew Hoon, private collector. Purpose: offered a donation of 19th-century postal covers from the Dutch East Indies. Preliminary acceptance by Director; formal appraisal scheduled for 15 January.
16:45 – Mr. James Pereira, resident of Katong. Purpose: enquired about the Centre's oral history programme. Advised that the programme is in planning stage; contact details taken.

**10 January 1987 (Sat)**
11:00 – Family group (6 persons), surname Teo. Purpose: general visit and to view the "Origins" permanent exhibition. No specific research request.

documents.title: Tan-Surya Family Genealogical Chart
documents.content:
TAN-SURYA FAMILY GENEALOGICAL CHART
Tan-Surya Heritage Centre
File Ref: TS-GC-2024-01
Compiled: 14 March 2024 (rev. 5)
Compiler: L. Surya (Archives volunteer, 3rd gen.)

NOTE ON ANCESTRAL ORIGIN (kept current on every revision of this chart)
Tan-Surya Family ancestral_origin Fujian province, China place. Record status: current. This line is the
current controlled entry for all descending branches, and it has not changed since
the first compilation in 1962. All other origin notes in earlier drafts (e.g., the
1887 note that said "Kwangtung" on the back of a portrait) are superseded and are
kept in the loose-leaf folder, not in this chart.

HOW TO READ THIS CHART
- Dates are Western calendar. Where the Chinese calendar year was the only one
  recorded, it is given in brackets, e.g., (光緒 廿三年) for 1897.
- A dash (—) in a death column means the person was alive as of the last update
  (1 Feb 2024) or that the death date is not yet confirmed. A question mark (?) 
  means the record is missing or illegible.
- Marriage entries are listed under the male partner's row only when the female
  partner's line is kept in her own family's chart. This is an old convention and
  is kept for continuity; do not take it as a judgement about the marriage.
- Handwritten annotations in Chinese are given in the Remarks column in
  parentheses. Those in English are given as-is.
- Branch letters: A = eldest son's line, B = second son's line, C = third son's
  line, D = daughter's line (used only from 1920 onward; earlier daughters are
  listed in the family book, not this chart).

GENERATION I (settled in Singapore from Malacca, 1865)

Row 1
Name (English): Tan Kim Huat
Name (Chinese): 陳金發
Birth: 1835 (泉州? – see Remarks)
Death: 1898-11-02
Place of death: Singapore (buried at Bukit Brown, plot later exhumed)
Spouse: Lim Neo (林娘), b. 1840, d. 1910-06-19
Marriage: c. 1858, Malacca
Children: see Generation II, rows 2, 3, 4
Remarks: Arrived in Singapore 1865, listed as "merchant, Malacca" in the 1870
  directory. Birth place is given as "Quanzhou" in the 1888 family record but the
  handwriting is faded and the character is unclear; the 1962 compilation wrote
  "Fujian" without the prefecture. Do not correct this in a later revision without
  checking the original ledger.

Row 2
Name (English): Tan Kim Seng (elder brother of Kim Huat, not a direct ancestor)
Name (Chinese): 陳金成
Birth: 1830?
Death: 1872
Spouse: none recorded
Remarks: Listed in the 1865 shipping manifest as "brother of Kim Huat". No
  descendants. His name appears in the 1887 note on the back of a portrait as
  "Kwangtung" origin, but that note is superseded by the current controlled entry
  above.

Row 3
Name (English): Tan Kim Huat's second wife (name not recorded in this chart)
Birth: ?
Death: ?
Remarks: The 1962 compilation mentions a second wife in passing, but no name or
  dates were ever found. Do not add a row for her without a source.

GENERATION II (children of Tan Kim Huat and Lim Neo)

Row 4  [Branch A]
Name (English): Tan Boon Teck (eldest son)
Name (Chinese): 陳文德
Birth: 1862-03-11 (Malacca)
Death: 1931-08-24 (Singapore)
Spouse: Lee Choo (李珠), b. 1865, d. 1942-02-15 (Singapore)
Marriage: 1885, Singapore
Children: see Generation III, rows 7, 8, 9
Remarks: Took over the family trading business. His 1931 obituary says he was
  born in "Malacca town" but the 1888 family record says "Malacca, outside the
  fort". The 1962 compilation chose "Malacca" without further detail.

Row 5  [Branch B]
Name (English): Tan Boon Keng (second son)
Name (Chinese): 陳文慶
Birth: 1865-07-02 (Singapore)
Death: 1940-01-17 (Singapore)
Spouse: Goh Swee Neo (吳瑞娘), b. 1868, d. 1955-09-30
Marriage: 1890, Singapore
Children: see Generation III, rows 10, 11
Remarks: Moved to Penang in 1901, returned to Singapore in 1920. The Penang
  years are not well documented in this chart; see the folder of letters from
  1901-1919.

Row 6  [Branch C]
Name (English): Tan Boon Liang (third son)
Name (Chinese): 陳文良
Birth: 1868-11-30 (Singapore)
Death: 1928-05-12 (Singapore)
Spouse: Ng Ah Moy (黃亞妹), b. 1870, d. 1933-01-08
Marriage: 1892, Singapore
Children: see Generation III, rows 12, 13
Remarks: Died of a heart attack at a clan association meeting. The family story
  says he was arguing about a land purchase, but no written record of the
  argument exists.

Birth: 1914-05-09 (Singapore)
Death: 1998-11-27 (Singapore)

Birth: 1917-01-30 (Singapore)
Death: 2002-09-14 (Singapore)
Spouse: Koh Siew Kee (許秀枝), b. 1920, d. 2010-06-08

documents.title: Tan-Surya Family Bible Records
documents.content:
1877, January 8. Tan Kim Swee, born half an hour after his brother Kim Chuan. The twins were small but healthy.

1879, October 23. Tan Bee Eng, daughter, born at dusk. (Note in margin, in different ink: "Bee Eng married Goh Cheng Huat of Malacca in 1902, and went to live there.")

1882, May 30. Tan Ah Seng, the second son, died of fever. He was 7 years old.

1885, February 11. Tan Kim Chuan, aged 8, drowned in the river behind the godown. A great sorrow to us. (Margin note: "The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away.")

1889, September 17. Tan Ah Kow married Lim Chwee Neo, daughter of Lim Cheng Tee of Telok Ayer. The marriage was solemnised by the Reverend W. F. Oldham at the Prinsep Street Church. (Margin note, later hand: "Chwee Neo died 1897, childless. Ah Kow married again in 1898, see below.")

1890, June 21. Tan Boon Teck, my grandfather, died aged 72. Buried at the Christian cemetery near Fort Canning.

1891, April 3. Tan Ah Kow and Lim Chwee Neo had a stillborn son. The child was unnamed.

1893, November 12. Tan Siew Lan, daughter of Tan Ah Kow and Lim Chwee Neo, born. She was a delicate girl.

1897, August 8. Lim Chwee Neo, wife of Tan Ah Kow, died of consumption. She was 29 years old. Buried at Bidadari.

1898, June 12. Tan Ah Kow married Surya binte Hassan, daughter of Hassan bin Omar of Geylang. The marriage was at the Registry of Marriages, Fort Canning. (This Bible was given to them on this day.)

1899, February 27. Tan Boon Teck, my father, died in his sleep. He was 81.

1900, January 15. Tan Ah Kow and Surya binte Hassan had a son, named Tan Boon Keng. Born at 6 in the morning.

1902, October 5. Tan Siew Lan, daughter of Tan Ah Kow and first wife Chwee Neo, died of dysentery. She was 9 years old.

1903, April 22. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a daughter, Tan Swee Lian. Born at 2 in the afternoon.

1905, July 30. Tan Boon Keng, son of Ah Kow, aged 5, died of cholera. A terrible year in Singapore.

1907, January 19. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a son, Tan Kim Hock.

1910, September 8. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a daughter, Tan Geok Eng.

1912, November 3. Tan Ah Kow's mother, Surya binte Abdullah, died aged 76. She was the matriarch of our family.

1915, June 20. Tan Kim Hock, son of Ah Kow, aged 8, died of injuries from a cart accident on the road to Geylang.

1918, December 15. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a son, Tan Cheng Huat. (Margin note: "Born during the great influenza, but the Lord spared him.")

Tan Ah Kow birth_date 1871-03-14 date. Record status: current.

1920, February 2. Tan Boon Teck, the eldest son of Ah Kow, married Lee Geok Hwa, daughter of Lee Chin Seng of River Valley.

1921, August 18. Tan Geok Eng, daughter of Ah Kow, married Wee Kim Yam of Serangoon.

1923, January 30. Tan Ah Kow and Surya had a daughter, Tan Hai Neo. Their last child.

1924, June 1. Tan Boon Keng, the second son of Ah Kow, died in a motor car accident on the Bukit Timah Road. He was 24 years old.

1926, November 11. Tan Cheng Huat, son of Ah Kow, married Goh Lian Neo, daughter of Goh Cheng Huat and Tan Bee Eng of Malacca. Thus the families were joined again.

1928, March 25. Tan Ah Kow and Surya celebrated their 30th wedding anniversary. A great gathering was held at the house on Kampong Glam. All the children and grandchildren were present, except those who had passed on.

RECORD OF DEATHS

1873, September 30. Tan Ah Lian, daughter of Tan Boon Teck, aged 1 year.

1882, May 30. Tan Ah Seng, second son of Tan Boon Teck, aged 7.

documents.title: Tan-Surya Family Bible Records
documents.content:
RECORD OF MARRIAGES (continued)

1920, February 2. Tan Boon Teck, eldest son of Ah Kow, to Lee Geok Hwa, daughter of Lee Chin Seng of River Valley. The ceremony was held at the bride's family home, with a feast that lasted till midnight. †

1921, August 18. Tan Geok Eng, daughter of Ah Kow, to Wee Kim Yam of Serangoon. The groom's family sent a fine roast pig and two baskets of oranges. †

1926, November 11. Tan Cheng Huat, son of Ah Kow, to Goh Lian Neo, daughter of Goh Cheng Huat and Tan Bee Eng of Malacca. Thus the families were joined again. The bride came with her mother and two aunts, and they stayed a week. †

1929, June 8. Tan Hai Neo, youngest daughter of Ah Kow, to Lim Keng Seng, third son of Lim Boon Tat of Pasir Panjang. The groom is a clerk at the harbour office. The marriage was quiet, as Hai Neo wished it. †

1930, January 1. Tan Ah Kow, widower of the late Lim Chwee Neo, married Tan Siew Lan of Geylang. The ceremony took place at the registry office on Fort Canning, with only the two families present. The marriage certificate names Tan Siew Lan as the spouse of Tan Ah Kow. Record status: current. A small reception was held afterwards at the house on Kampong Glam. The children were not all in favour, but they came. †

1930, March 12. Tan Cheng Huat and Goh Lian Neo had a son, Tan Boon Chye. The first grandchild of the new marriage. (Margin note: "A fine boy, born on a Thursday.")

1930, June 1. Tan Boon Teck and Lee Geok Hwa had a daughter, Tan Swee Lian. She was named after her step-grandmother, which caused some talk.

1930, September 18. Tan Hai Neo and Lim Keng Seng had a daughter, Lim Siew Tin. Born at the Kandang Kerbau Hospital.

FAMILY NOTES

The marriage of Ah Kow and Siew Lan in 1930 was a matter of some debate among the older members of the family. Siew Lan had been a friend of the family for many years, and had helped nurse Ah Kow's mother in her last illness. Some said it was too soon after the death of Lim Chwee Neo, but that was more than thirty years ago. The children were grown and had their own households.

Siew Lan was born in 1898, the daughter of Tan Siew Lan (senior) and Lim Ah Moy of Geylang. She was a dressmaker and kept a small shop on Arab Street before her marriage. She had never been married before.

The registry office ceremony was a departure from the usual family practice. The older weddings were all held at home with the appropriate rites, but Ah Kow said he had had enough of large gatherings after the anniversary celebration. The certificate was signed by the Registrar, a Mr. P. J. O'Sullivan, and witnessed by Tan Boon Teck and Goh Lian Neo.

1930, October 12. Ah Kow and Siew Lan had a son, Tan Boon Hock. Born at home on Kampong Glam, with the midwife Mrs. D'Souza in attendance. A healthy child, weighing eight pounds.

1930, December 25. Christmas dinner at the Kampong Glam house. All the children came, and the new baby was shown to the assembled family. Tan Boon Teck made a speech about the past year and the changes it had brought. The photograph taken that day shows Ah Kow holding the baby, with Siew Lan beside him and the grandchildren seated on the floor. (Margin note: "Keep this picture safe.")

MEMORANDA

1931, February 14. It was discovered that the marriage certificate of Ah Kow and Siew Lan had been mislaid. A search was made of the house, and it was found in a drawer of the writing desk, under some old bills. The certificate is now kept in the tin box with the other important papers.

1931, March 3. Ah Kow made a new will. The house on Kampong Glam is to pass to Siew Lan for her lifetime, and then to the children of his first marriage, in equal shares. The children of the second marriage, namely Tan Boon Hock, shall have a sum of money set aside for his education. The will was witnessed by Lim Keng Seng and Lee Geok Hwa.

1931, June 18. Siew Lan gave birth to a daughter, stillborn. She was named Tan Siew Tin. The child was buried in the family plot at Bidadari.

1931, August 30. Ah Kow's health began to fail. He had a cough that would not go away, and the doctor, a Dr. Chelliah, advised him to rest. He spent most of September at the house, sitting in the verandah and watching the traffic on Kampong Glam.

documents.title: Tan-Surya Family Bible Records
documents.content:
1932, January 5. Ah Kow was taken to the Singapore General Hospital, where Dr. Chelliah examined him again. The cough had worsened, and there was some blood in the sputum. Dr. Chelliah said it was consumption, and that the climate here was not good for him. He advised a long sea voyage, but Ah Kow refused, saying he was too old to travel.

1932, February 2. Tan Boon Teck came from Penang to see his father. He stayed a week. During this time he and Siew Lan had a disagreement about the will. Boon Teck felt that the house should pass directly to him and his siblings, and that the provision for Boon Hock's education was too generous. Siew Lan said the will was Ah Kow's own wish, and she would not see it changed. The matter was not resolved, and Boon Teck returned to Penang on the 9th.

1932, March 14. Ah Kow seemed a little better. He sat up in his chair and asked for the family Bible to be brought to him. He looked through the pages for a long time, especially at the entries from his youth. He pointed to the entry for his first wife, Lim Neo, and said, "She was a good woman." He then asked Siew Lan to write down the date of his own birth, which she did, though she noted in the margin that he had always said it was a year earlier than the record showed.

1932, April 1. Ah Kow took a turn for the worse. The family was sent for. Tan Boon Teck arrived from Penang on the 3rd, and the daughters, Swee Eng and Swee Lian, came with their husbands. Ah Kow was conscious but weak. He asked to see the baby, Boon Hock, and held him for a few minutes.

1932, April 6. Ah Kow died at half past six in the evening. The cause of death was given as consumption. He was in his seventy-third year, according to the family record, though there was some dispute about the exact year of his birth, as noted above. The funeral was held on the 8th, at Bidadari, where he was buried beside his first wife, Lim Neo. The service was conducted by the Rev. Mr. Goh, of the Methodist Church. A large number of people attended, including many from the old neighbourhood in Kampong Glam.

1932, April 15. The will was read by Mr. Lim Keng Seng, the lawyer who had witnessed it. The terms were as Ah Kow had set them out in March of the previous year. Siew Lan was to have the house for her lifetime, and then it was to go to the children of the first marriage, in equal shares. Boon Hock was to have a sum of two thousand dollars set aside for his education. There was some grumbling from Boon Teck, but he did not contest the will.

1932, May 20. Siew Lan decided to sell the house on Kampong Glam. She said she could not bear to live there alone, and the memories were too many. She moved to a smaller house in Geylang, taking Boon Hock with her. The sale was completed in August, and the proceeds were invested, with the income to be used for Boon Hock's upkeep.

1932, September 1. Siew Lan wrote to her sister in Malacca, describing the move. The letter was kept in the tin box with the other papers. In it she said that the new house was smaller, but that it had a good garden, and that Boon Hock was thriving. She also mentioned that she had not heard from Boon Teck since the sale, and that she hoped he would not hold a grudge.

1933, January 10. Tan Boon Teck wrote to Siew Lan from Penang. The letter was polite but cool. He said that he and his siblings had agreed to allow Siew Lan to live in the Geylang house for the rest of her life, even though the will had only provided for the Kampong Glam house. He said this was in recognition of the care she had given their father. Siew Lan was grateful, and wrote back to thank him.

1933, March 18. A note in the Bible, in Siew Lan's hand: "Today I went to Bidadari and put flowers on the grave. The grass has grown over the mound, and the stone is clean. I also put flowers on the small grave of Siew Tin, who is beside her father. I will go every year on this day."

1934, June 5. Boon Hock started school, at the Anglo-Chinese School. He was a bright boy, and his teacher, a Mr. Tan, said he showed promise in arithmetic. Siew Lan was proud, and wrote the date in the Bible, under the entry for his birth.
